title: Benchmark workshop - workload fidelity & KV cache synthesis - Hydra Systems
summary: Working session to align on a repeatable apples-to-apples benchmark: define prompt sets, load generation approach, KV cache warmup protocol, batching/quantization knobs, and measurement artifacts. Agreed next steps include running a short replay test and sharing a benchmark runbook + spreadsheet.

Hydra to provide a 24-hour representative request trace and sample prompt groups by 2026-11-05

transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-10-28 15:00 UTC | Duration 72m | Attendees: Lena Ortiz (Redwood AE), Marcus Hale (Redwood SE), Ivy Chen (Redwood), Priya Menon (Hydra CTO), Darren Cole (Head of ML), Samir Khan (Infra), Aisha Patel (SRE)

[00:00] Lena Ortiz: alright everyone uh thanks for joining. quick goal for today is to lock down a benchmark protocol we can both run. especially around kv cache warmup and load replay tradeoffs.

[00:18] Priya Menon: yeah thanks lena. we wanna make sure our perf story is repeatable. we got inconsistent tail latency numbers last quarter when we moved a model into prod.

[00:30] Marcus Hale: totally, and hi all. i put together a starter runbook that tries to address warmup bias, synthetic vs replay, and tokenization normalization. i'll share after. couple things to call out up front: prefix caching patterns and batching are the biggest source of variance.

[00:48] Darren Cole: can you define prefix caching? i think some folks use that to mean different things — is it kv cache + prefix dedupe or just prefix-based reuse?

[00:56] Marcus Hale: good point. our shorthand: "prefix/KV cache" is the model kv key-value reuse for autoregressive generation; prefix dedupe is a higher level app pattern. for benchmarks we want raw kv-hit rate measurement. so we instrument hits per request and bytes saved.

[01:12] Aisha Patel: and we also have an infra constraint — when we run onprem in our VPC we see cold starts because our autoscaler scales in aggressively overnight. how do we simulate that?

[01:22] Ivy Chen: that's why we include a warmup protocol. recommended pattern: 30 minute steady-state warmup where you replay unique user traces scaled to 30% of target qps, then ramp to target load. that helps fill kv caches and warms GPU kernels.

[01:40] Priya Menon: 30 minutes sounds long; we have to show something to execs next week. any shorter alternative that is still valid?

[01:47] Marcus Hale: you can do a micro-warmup for demos: run the most frequent 1,000 prompts with same token distribution as production for 5-10 minutes. but micro-warmup will not reflect cold-start tail latencies. so you must call out the scope in the report.

[02:05] Darren Cole: talking about prompts, we have multiple families — short completion queries, doc-summarize long inputs, and chat-style multi-turn. how do we make an apples-to-apples prompt set?

[02:15] Lena Ortiz: our approach: stratified prompt sampling. pick N examples per family preserving token length distribution and slot in canonical system messages for chat. export tokenized lengths with the prompt set so everyone uses the same tokenizer.

[02:30] Samir Khan: tokenizer differences have bitten us. our pretokenization in our app is different than downstream inference; we need to agree on the tokenizer model and exact BPE config.

[02:40] Marcus Hale: yes — step one: agree on tokenizer binaries (e.g., tiktoken v0.4 with model xyz vocab) and include a checksum in the runbook. we also recommend storing sample token counts alongside the raw text.

[02:55] Speaker 2 (maybe customer): ummm, one more question on load generation — replay vs synthetic? which gives more faithful results?

[03:02] Marcus Hale: both have pros/cons. replay preserves real-world distributions including prefix reuse (which affects kv cache), session stickiness, and latencies from upstream. but pure replay can leak PII unless scrubbed. synthetic lets you control variables and explore corner cases but may miss subtle correlations. our recommended hybrid: replay critical traces for fidelity + synthetic stress runs for capacity planning.

[03:28] Priya Menon: scrubbed replay is doable. we'll anonymize user IDs but maintain session grouping. is there a recommended tool?

[03:34] Marcus Hale: we have an internal harness we can share; open-source options include wrk-style replay tools and a small python harness that replays respecting inter-arrival times. i'll add the repo link to the runbook.

[03:46] Aisha Patel: on measurement: what metrics should we report? p50/p90/p99, tail latencies, throughput, and cost right?

[03:55] Ivy Chen: include percent of requests served from kv cache, average token-per-request, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, and memory pressure. also record kernel fallback events and quantization-induced errors.

[04:10] Darren Cole: quantization-induced errors — can you expand? we tried int8 and saw some exact-match drop in QA tasks. how do we measure quality regressions that matter to product?

[04:18] Marcus Hale: for quality you need a small eval set per prompt family. measure micro- and macro-metrics: BLEU/ROUGE if you use them, but more importantly task-specific metrics (QA EM, F1, or human evals for generation). run the eval after quantizing and compare against FP16 baseline. we also recommend a noise-injection A/B to check degradation distribution.

[04:38] Priya Menon: and is quantization deterministic across runtimes? i mean would int8 on your runtime compare to int8 on another cloud vendor?

[04:46] Marcus Hale: not always. quant kernels and dequant strategies differ. for apples-to-apples we recommend comparing FP16 vs quant on the same runtime and hardware family; if you need cross-vendor compare, document kernel versions and provide test vectors (golden outputs) for a handful of prompts.

[05:05] Samir Khan: hardware note — we run both A100s and a small Ampere flavor on prem; and we sometimes use mixed CPU/GPU tokenization pre-processing. how should we normalize?

[05:16] Ivy Chen: key is to separate infra measurement from model inference. capture pre- and post-inference timing. for cross-hardware, report per-token latency normalized by peak throughput and include raw CPU/GPU specs. also, list batch sizes and kernel versions.

[05:31] Lena Ortiz: regarding batching: continuous batching vs fixed batch windows — what does hydra prefer?

[05:38] Priya Menon: we prefer predictable tail latencies, so fixed small windows were appealing, but that hurts throughput/cost.

[05:45] Marcus Hale: Right — continuous batching (opportunistic) yields better utilization and cost but can increase variability. For benchmarks include two modes: latency-priority (small fixed batches, lower batching latency) and throughput-priority (continuous batching, higher throughput). report both curves.

[06:02] Darren Cole: about KV hit rate — is it measured per-token or per-request?

[06:08] Marcus Hale: measure both. per-token gives you granularity on how many KV slots saved; per-request shows how many requests benefited. We instrument hit-rate, hit-bytes, and cache occupancy over time.

[06:20] Priya Menon: what about deterministic replay? we need to get exact same sequence for repeatability across runs.

[06:26] Marcus Hale: determinism is tricky because of scheduling jitter and GPU nondeterminism. for better repeatability: pin CPU affinity, reserve dedicated nodes, fix batch sizes and seeds, and disable stochastic sampling in the model (use greedy or fixed-top-k if applicable). still you'll see small numeric diffs; that's why we run statistical multiple trials and report confidence intervals.

[06:47] Aisha Patel: for VPC/on-prem security we need to test with mTLS and KMS in the loop. any pitfalls?

[06:53] Marcus Hale: yes — encryption adds CPU crypto overhead for small inference sizes. measure both with and without KMS calls (cache keys locally vs call KMS each request). also confirm network egress / NAT latency if cross-region. we'll capture that in the runbook as separate "secure mode" runs.

[07:10] Priya Menon: can we embed SLO checks into the harness so failures are flagged?

[07:14] Ivy Chen: absolutely — the runbook suggests a small post-processing script that computes SLO pass/fail for p90 < X ms and p99 < Y ms and outputs a markdown summary. we'll include threshold templates.

[07:25] Darren Cole: any caution on sample sizes? we don't want to run a 48-hour test every time.

[07:31] Marcus Hale: for tail estimates you need enough samples. p99 needs many events; we recommend at least 100k requests for stable p99 in high-QPS workloads or run multiple shorter windows and aggregate. for lower qps, longer windows are required. we give guidance in the runbook.

[07:45] Lena Ortiz: ok let's talk artifacts — Marcus, you'll share runbook + harness link. We'll include: prompt set repo, tokenizer checksum, sample traces, spreadsheet with baseline columns (FP16 baseline, int8, batch configs, warmup protocol).

[07:59] Marcus Hale: yep i'll push a draft and a sample spreadsheet. I'll also include a small golden output set so Hydra can validate cross-vendor comparisons.

[08:08] Priya Menon: timeline wise, we want first pilot before 2026-11-12. is that feasible?

[08:14] Marcus Hale: yes, if we get traces and keys this week. we can run a 2–4 hour replay pilot and share results in 48 hours.

[08:22] Samir Khan: regarding access, we'll do a temporary allowlist and share stub creds. do you need anything special for the pilot in terms of network?

[08:29] Marcus Hale: IP allowlist + minimal VPC peering is fine. if you want private deployment testing we can use a short-lived dedicated cluster in your subnet. we'll need the kubecontext and a support engineer call for that.

[08:44] Aisha Patel: one more question — how to present cost comparisons? we want cost per 1M tokens but also cost per successful request at SLO. any recommended columns?

[08:52] Ivy Chen: include cost per token, cost per request, effective cost at target latency (e.g., cost when maintaining p90 < target). show tradeoff plots. we'll add sample cost calc in the spreadsheet.

[09:05] Priya Menon: sounds good. to close, can we summarize action items?

[09:10] Lena Ortiz: sure. marcus to share runbook and harness link by 11/02; darren to export 24h trace and tokenization notes by 11/05; samir to confirm network allowlist by 11/04. hydra to pick preferred pilot week (week of 11/08).

[09:26] Marcus Hale: and i'll include sample golden outputs and spreadsheet templates.

[09:31] Priya Menon: thanks all, useful session. we'll follow up in the thread.

[09:35] Lena Ortiz: thanks everyone — we'll send calendar invite for the pilot once we get the traces. bye.

End of transcript. Links referenced: runbook draft (internal) - https://redwood.example.com/runbooks/benchmarks/hydra-draft , harness repo - https://github.com/redwood-inference/benchmark-harness , sample spreadsheet - https://redwood.example.com/spreadsheets/hydra-benchmark-template.xlsx
